item.title: Workflow Discussion
item.description:
Workflow Discussion

2026–04–12

Neovim Config

So what makes a good workflow?

The main question that must be answered when writing a workflow is what’s the goal?

My main function for this work flow follows a couple of guidelines :

  • Speed, everything should be one or two key presses away.
  • Durability, everything must be consistent and resilient to changes.

So here’s the stack I’ve settled on :

Task Tech
Windows i31
Text Editing Neovim
Terminals Kitty
Sessions Tmux

After experimenting with a few window management options like OXWM, DWM, and Hyprland I’d ultimately end up settling on i3. For a couple reasons :

  • i3 is so simple to configure, DWM required tons of recompilation and was thus incredibly slow to iterate with. Whenever I wanted to test another change or breakout window it would require tons of patching and modification in Xephyr. I3 on the other hand allows for 90% of it’s config to be done on a singular file and it’s api is incredibly accessible for simple shell scripting to control the rest of it’s behavior.
  • I dislike wayland because it’s too new for not much gain, the time I’d need to invest into learning wayland doesn’t seem to offer many real advantages. Sorry Niri fans
  • The tiling on i3 just flows best with my way of thinking, especially with a small autotiling script I wrote. The manager allows for a great mix of program based workspace pinning, automatic tiling, and gaps / vanity features with picom

Using Neovim follows pretty intuitively. I am not smart enough to use emacs, and large electron based apps like vscode are terrible for battery, performance, and aura.

There’s not much of a reason for kitty, it was honestly the first terminal emulator I used and it always worked well. Never really found a reason to go out and find a new terminal emulator. It also has a very nice color api!

Tmux is used for 2 things, multiplexing in kitty and session persistence. I use the splitting in Tmux because it handles the text movements and artifacting even better than the native panes. But the main benefit of Tmux comes from it’s session persistence combined with searchable sessions. I write extensively about this in my post here

  1. Much to the chagrin of wayland loving John and others  ↩︎

item.title: TMUX Sessionizing!
item.description:
TMUX Sessionizing!

2026–05–20

Mux and motivation

Link to all code

Video demo

I’ve always used a ton of bash scripts for my main work flows. From generating homework templates from my LaTeX days to parsing webpages to form my local homework due deadline calenders. But recently as my Inpirion has begun dying a slow and painful death after 3 years of use, new problems have emerged.

With the occasional random poweroffs and inability to sleep without fully shutting off, I’m not longer able to just leave each of my projects open on a different i3 tags. So I’ve begun exploring an old rite of passage for tiling window manager using vimmers, TMUX

My main desire for TMUX comes from it’s ability to maintain and hold sessions in a small format that can be accessed later (using a script). These persistent sessions are useful for a few reasons :

  • Quick on the fly customization that you can’t achieve with standard text based layout sessionizers.
  • Multiple types of multiplexing, whether panes windows or scrolls. Although I typically only ever use panes
  • Better resizing text handling than the built in kitty options.
  • The sessions take up very little space and can be nearly constantly updated or stored using plugins like resurrect and continuum

So how do we go about this? The most famous starting point for a sessionizing script would be the well known Primeagain script. But this script has a few problems in my opinion,

  • The ability to make multiple sessions on the same project seems to be a negative and could only lead to confusion.
  • There’s no reason to outline multiple entrances into the same directory (using the [tmux] tag doesn’t improve this).
  • It’s lacking the ability to quickly pull from remote repos / make new sessions in new local directories.

So here I can introduced an improved sessionizing script that fulfills the original goals of the primeagen’s script while being just slightly longer.

Here you have a few options and improvements :

  • Paths are cleaned up to be shorter and cleaner
  • You can directly clone any codeberg or gitlab repo just by directly entering it into the fzf field, where you can then select any destination from the home / current directory.
  • If an active session exists in the parent directory to one you are looking,
  • No need for a config file!

item.title: Starting with the Tang 9k FPGA.
item.description:
Starting with the Tang 9k FPGA.

2026–03–23

First Purchases and Inspiration :

After 2 semesters of courses covering FPGA and verilog development in computer architecture, I’ve finally decided to purchase my own Tang Nano 9k to start on a couple of extracurricular projects.

Why the Tang Nano 9k?

The Tang Nano 9k is frequently compared to it’s slightly larger brother, the 20k. But the difference between the two is not significant enough to warrant the extra 3 weeks of delivery I would have had to wait if I had purchased that.

The Plan

I’ll start by implementing the heavily reduced instruction set defined in the tutorials by Lushay Labs.

item.title: The first day with the Tang Nano 9K
item.description:
The first day with the Tang Nano 9K

2026–03–28

Getting started!

Link to all code

So the board has arrived! But I can’t be bothered to use the proprietary IDE / toolchain that the brand provides. So instead, I’ll be using the oss-cad-suite to generate bitstreams then openFPGALoader to program the Tang Nano.

But in other news, I was able to get the whole thing working and get a nice blink / counter on the FPGA. Next up will be properly soldering it and tying it to some LED’s on a breadboard.
